div.p: Background: A growing body of evidence suggests that low levels of physical activity (PA) and high levels of sedentary behavior (SB) are associated with an increased risk of adverse health outcomes in patients. Despite the objective of cardiovascular rehabilitation (CR) programs to increase PA and decrease SB levels, many patients continue to show low PA and high SB levels following their discharge from CR. The objective of the present study was to examined the levels of PA and SB following an outpatient CR program and to examine their motivational and emotional health-related correlates. PA and SB levels, along with motivational and health-related characteristics, were compared between outpatients and control participants who did not require care.

Methods: The study included 119 participants: 68 CR patients (M age 57.76±10.76; 86.76% males) and 51 control participants matched on age (M age 57.35±6.33 years; 45.10% males). Accelerometers were used to assess PA and SB during the rst week post-discharge for outpatients and during a typical week for controls. Validated scales were employed to measure motivational (i.e., perceived capabilities, affective and instrumental attitudes, intention, approach-avoidance tendencies) and emotional health-related (i.e., anxiety, depressive symptoms, fatigue, pain intensity) factors.

Results: CR patients spent an average of 60.21 (±34.79) min of moderate-to-vigorous PA (MVPA), and 548.69 (±58.64) min of SB per day. They engaged in 18 more minutes of MVPA per day than controls (p =.038). Univariate and multivariate regressions indicated that positive affective attitudes were associated with higher MVPA (b = 10.32, R 2 = 0.07, p =.029). Additionally, males spent more time in SB than females (b = 40.54, R 2 = 0.09, p =.045). Univariate and multivariate logistic regressions showed that meeting the World Health Organization's weekly guidelines for MVPA was associated with higher perceived capabilities toward PA and more positive affective attitudes (OR = 1.17, p =.030; OR = 1.26, p <.001, respectively). Interaction tests showed no signi cant differences in these results between outpatients and controls.
Conclusion: These ndings underscore the importance of motivational factors in PA levels following a CR program.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Physical activity (PA), de ned as "any bodily movement produced by skeletal muscles that results in energy expenditure [1]", is an integral part of cardiac rehabilitation (CR) programs [2,3]. Exercise-based CR has been shown to provide numerous bene ts, including increased exercise capacity and quality of life, as well as decreased cardiovascular mortality and the risk of hospital readmissions [3,4]. Conversely, sedentary behavior (SB), de ned as any waking behavior characterized by an energy expenditure ≤ 1.5 Metabolic Equivalent Tasks, such as sitting and lying down [5], has been associated with several adverse health outcomes in patients. Evidence has shown that patients with coronary artery disease who adopt high levels of SB (4-8 hours per day) have a 62% higher mortality rate compared to those who adopt in SB for less than 4 hours per day [6]. Although CR programs aim to increase PA and decrease SB levels, many patients still exhibit low PA and high SB levels after discharge from CR [7][8][9].

For example, only 20% of CR patients met the PA targets of 150-300 min of moderate-to-vigorous PA (MVPA) per week [10] six months after discharge [7]. Furthermore, Bakker et al. [9] showed that cardiovascular disease patients adopt higher SB levels before and up to 2 months after participating in a CR program, in comparison to healthy controls. However, while PA and SB have demonstrated independent health effects [11][12][13], few studies have examined these two behaviors simultaneously. Thus, measuring PA and SB levels in patients after discharge from CR and identifying their correlates is warranted.

Anchored in a dual-process perspective, it has been argued that two types of cognitive processes can in uence PA behaviors [14][15][16]. The rst type, referred to as deliberative process, is intentional, effortful, controllable, and conscious [17]. The second type, referred to as automatic process, is typically de ned as unconscious, effortless, unintended, and uncontrollable [18]. Deliberative motivational factors, such as intention, perceived capability to engage in a behavior, or attitudes, are key for predicting engagement in exercise and PA and reducing SB levels [15,19]. In the context of CR, Bierbauer et al. [8] showed that higher intention toward PA was associated with greater PA levels after discharge from CR. In the same vein, Bermudez et al. [2] found that patients with higher affective attitudes toward PA (i.e., evaluating PA as pleasant) had higher intentions toward PA and participated in more light-intensity PA after discharge from CR. In addition to these deliberative motivational factors, recent studies have shown that automatic motivational factors may further explain patients' engagement in PA. For instance, Chevance et al. [20] found that a positive automatic affective evaluation toward PA was signi cantly associated with higher PA levels (β = .29) after pulmonary rehabilitation. Recently, Cheval et al. [21] suggested that approachavoidance tendencies, which refer to the automatic preparation of the organism to execute a motor pattern in the direction of a behavior [22] ,could partly explain PA engagement after a CR program.

In addition to motivational factors,, the presence of depression, anxiety, or pain, has also been associated with lower levels of PA following a CR program [7]. In the context of patients with advanced cancer, with chronic kidney disease, and with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, perceived fatigue appeared to be a substantial barrier to PA [23][24][25]. However, the extent to which fatigue, PA, and SB are related in patients with cardiovascular disease after discharge from CR remains unknown. Taken together, these studies suggest that considering both deliberative and automatic motivational factors for PA, as well as emotional health-related factors, may provide a comprehensive perspective on PA and SB levels after CR. However, to the best of our knowledge, the role of automatic motivational processes in the regulation of PA and SB among patients with cardiovascular disease has been largely neglected.

Finally, while previous work has shown that emotional health-related factors are associated with PA levels [7], little is known about the relationship between emotional health-related variables and SB levels.

The primary objective of this study was to assess accelerometer-based PA and SB levels during the rst week following a 6-week outpatients CR program and to examine their motivational (i.e., intention, perceived capability, attitudes, and approach-avoidance tendencies) and emotional health-related (i.e., depressive symptoms, anxiety, fatigue, and pain intensity) correlates. Additionally, it has been suggested that the key motivational process involved in the regulation of PA and SB may differ between CR patients and a healthy control population [21,26]. Therefore, an additional aim of this study was to compare the PA and SB levels, as well as the motivational and health-related characteristics, of patients following an outpatient CR program, with those of community-dwelling control healthy participants, who did not require care.

div.head: Study Design and Participants
div.p: The sample size was initially estimated to ensure su cient power to detect an effect in the Improving Physical Activity (IMPACT) trial (see Cheval et al. [21]) for the IMPACT trial protocol. The IMPACT trial, carried out at Geneva University Hospitals (Switzerland), is a phase 3 single-center, placebo, triple-blind randomized controlled trial that enrolled participants from an outpatient CR program. The detailed content of the CR program is described in Supplementary Material 1. The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of Geneva Canton, Switzerland (reference number: CCER2019-02257).

The present study analyzed a dataset consisting of 68 CR patients. Furthermore, 51 additional community-dwelling control participants were recruited using snowball sampling. Community-dwelling participants were included if they were 40 years or older, matching the minimum age of outpatients, had no contraindication to PA, and were not receiving medical care. PA and SB levels were measured via accelerometer (Actigraph GT3x+; Pensacola, USA) for seven consecutive days during the week following discharge from the CR program for the outpatients and for seven consecutive days for the control participants. Motivational and emotional health-related variables were assessed before measuring PA and SB for all participants.

div.head: Measures Physical Activity and Sedentary Behavior Outcomes
div.p: The usual level of PA, de ned as the amount of time spent being physically active in a typical week during free time, was assessed using the Saltin-Grimby PA Level Scale [27]. Outpatients were asked to report their PA levels for a typical week before the onset of the health problem that necessitated the CR.
Participants were categorized as (a) physically inactive, (b) engaging in some PA, (c) engaging in regular PA, or (d) engaging in regular high-intensity training.

Participants were asked to wear the accelerometer only during waking hours. Daily data were included if wearing time was ≥ 10 waking hours per day [28]. Data were included if at least 4 days met the aforementioned conditions and included one weekend day [29]. Additionally, daily PA and SB levels were self-reported using the short form of the International Physical Activity Questionnaire [30]. We used accelerometer-based daily time spent engaging in PAs of light, moderate, vigorous, and moderate-to-vigorous intensity, as well as the number of steps, as indicators of PA levels. Finally, accelerometerbased daily time spent engaging in SB was used as an indicator of SB levels.

div.head: Motivational Factors
div.p: Perceived capability to engage in PA was assessed using the following item from the Patients-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS [31]): "To what extent are you able to perform daily physical activities such as walking, climbing stairs, or moving a chair?". Participants answered on a scale from 1 (not at all) to 5 (completely).

Intention to be physically active was assessed using the following item: "I intend to do more physical activity in the near future [21]." Participants answered on a scale from 1 (totally disagree) to 10 (totally agree).

Instrumental and affective attitudes were assessed using the following two items "Would you say physical activity is something …". Participants answered each item on a scale from 1 (useless) to 10 (useful) for instrumental attitudes, and from 1 (unpleasant) to 10 (pleasant) for affective attitudes [32,33].

Automatic approach-avoidance tendencies toward PA and SB were assessed using the Visual-Approach/Avoidance-by-the-Self-Task (VAAST [34]). The VAAST protocol is explained in more detail in Supplementary Material 2.

div.head: Emotional Health-Related Factors
div.p: Anxiety, depression, fatigue, and pain intensity were assessed using PROMIS items. Anxiety was assessed using the following two items: "In the past 7 days, I felt scared" and "In the last 7 days, I found it hard to focus on anything other than my anxiety." Participants answered each item on a scale from 1 (never) to 10 (always). Items were averaged (Pearson correlation = 0.61). Depression was assessed using the following four items: "In the past 7 days, I felt..." "useless," "powerless," "desperate," and "depressed." Participants answered each item on a scale from 1 (never) to 10 (always). The items were averaged (Cronbach's α = 0.81).

Fatigue was assessed using the following three items: "In the past 7 days, I felt tired," "In the last 7 days, I had a hard time starting things because I felt tired," and "In the past 7 days, how tired do you feel on average?". Participants answered each item on a scale from 1 (not at all) to 5 (very much). The items were averaged (Cronbach's α = 0.90).
Pain intensity was assessed using the following item: "How would you rate your average pain level?".
Participants answered on a scale from 1 (no pain) to 5 (worst pain imaginable).

Measures of additional health-related variables such as perceived mobility, limitations in activities of daily living, limitations in instrumental activities of daily living, global physical and mental health, life satisfaction, indication for enrollment in the outpatient CR, left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), maximal aerobic power (MAP), abdominal circumference, glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c), triglycerides, low-density lipoprotein (LDL)-cholesterol, blood pressure, smoking, and the presence of comorbidity are described in Supplementary Material 3.

div.head: Descriptive Statistical Analyses
div.p: First, we conducted descriptive analyses of the participants' characteristics and compared them between the outpatient and control participants using independent t tests for numerical variables and chi-squared tests for categorical variables. Additional analyses were carried out to compare outpatients' motivational and health-related characteristics measured at the beginning and at the end of the CR using independent t tests. Third, we estimated the levels of PA and SB for seven consecutive days during the week following discharge from the CR program for the outpatients and for seven consecutive days for control participants. Fourth, we compared the levels of PA and SB in outpatients with those in control participants using independent t tests.

div.head: Univariate and Multivariate Regression Analyses
div.p: First, we conducted univariate and multivariate regression analyses to examine the associations of motivational (i.e., perceived capabilities to engage in PA, intention to engage in PA, instrumental and affective attitudes toward PA, and approach-avoidance tendencies) and emotional health-related factors (i.e., depressive symptoms, anxiety, fatigue, and pain intensity) with PA and SB levels. Outpatients' motivational and emotional health-related factors measured at the end of the CR were used in the univariate and multivariate analyses. In the univariate and multivariate regression analyses, interaction terms were tested between participant type (i.e., outpatient vs. control) and the motivational and emotional health-related factors to examine whether the associations of motivational and emotional health-related factors with the levels of PA and sedentary behavior SB differed between outpatients and control participants. The independent variables were standardized. Finally, logistic regression analyses were conducted to determine the odds ratio associated with meeting the recommended level of PA (i.e., 150 min of MVPA per week [10]) based on the motivational and emotional health-related factors. Statistical assumptions, including normality of residuals, linearity, multicollinearity, and undue in uence, were checked, and met for all models using the Performance R package [35].

div.head: Descriptive results
div.p: Table 1 shows the results of the sample characteristics. A total of 119 participants (68 patients enrolled in an CR program [86.76% males; M age = 57.76 ± 10.76 years] and 51 community-dwelling control participants [45.10% males; M age = 57.35 ± 6.33 years]) were included in the study. The mean patient LVEF was 52.87% (± 10.49), and most patients were enrolled in the CR program for acute coronary syndrome (40.30% non-ST elevation and 26.87% ST elevation). Before the cardiovascular event that prompted CR, outpatients self-reported signi cantly lower PA levels than control participants. The emotional health-related variables showed that at the beginning of the CR, outpatients showed signi cantly higher perceived fatigue. Outpatients self-reported a signi cantly higher number of IADLs, greater di culty with mobility, lower global physical and mental health, and life satisfaction compared to control participants. The PA-related motivational variables showed that at the beginning of the CR, outpatients had signi cantly lower perceived capability and affective attitudes than control participants. No statistically signi cant differences were observed in approach-avoidance tendencies toward PA and SB between outpatients and control participants. Table 2 presents the PA and SB levels for the outpatients and control participants. During the rst week following the rehabilitation period, only 17 out of 68 outpatients and 42 out of 51 control participants had a valid accelerometer data (see Fig. 1 for the ow diagram). As a result, the PA and SB levels were analyzed for 59 participants. The results showed that, in the week following the CR, the outpatients spent an average of 548.69 (± 58.64) min per day in SB, 211.16 (± 60.83) min in light-intensity PA, 57.85 (± 34.68) min in moderate-intensity PA, 2.28 (± 3.67) min in vigorous-intensity PA. Thus, on average, outpatients spent 60.21 (± 34.79) min per day in MVPA, with 88.2% of them meeting the recommended weekly level of 150 min of MVPA. Control participants displayed a similar overall pattern, although they spent slightly more time in light-intensity PA (253.77 ± 69.11, p = .035) and slightly less time in moderateintensity PA (37.46 ± 25.03, p = .014). On average, control participants spent signi cantly less time (41.78 ± 2.088, p = .038) per day in MVPA compared to outpatients, with 71.4% of them meeting the recommended 150 min per week of MVPA (p = .310). Finally, outpatients averaged 10083.00 (± 4493.27) steps per day, while the controls averaged 8785.02 (± 3424.07) steps per day. However, this difference was not statistically signi cant (p = .237). div.head: Sensitivity Power Analyses
div.p: Following Lakens' [36] recommendations, a sensitivity curve was plotted for a linear univariate regression, with an alpha level of .05 and a sample size of 59 participants (i.e., number of participants with complete device-based data). This allowed us to assess the effect sizes that can be detected across a range of desired power levels [36]. Powers between 33%, which aligns with the limit of studies that are considered insu ciently powerful [37], and 90% were analyzed. For an univariate regression, the sensitivity curve showed that our study had between 33% and 90% power of detecting an effect size between f 2 = .04; or R 2 = .04 and f 2 = .18; or R 2 = .16, respectively. For a multivariate regression with two predictors (i.e., affective attitudes and participant type), the sensitivity curve showed that our study had between 33% and 90% power of detecting an effect size between f 2 = .06; or R 2 = .06 and f 2 = .25; or R 2 = .20, respectively. For a multivariate regression with three predictors (i.e., sex, pain intensity, participant type), the sensitivity curve showed that our study had between 33% and 90% power of detecting an effect size between f 2 = .07; or R 2 = .06 and f 2 = .29; or R 2 = .23, respectively. Additionally, a sensitivity curve was plotted for a logistic regression, with an alpha level of .05 and a sample size of 59 participants. The sensitivity curve showed that, for a positive effect of the independent variable on PA and SB levels, our study had between 33% and 90% power of detecting an effect size between OR = 1.50 and OR = 2.70, respectively. The sensitivity curve showed that, for a negative effect of the independent variable on PA and SB levels, our study had between 33% and 90% power of detecting an effect size between OR = 0.66 and OR = 0.37, respectively. The sensitivity curves are available in Supplementary Material 7, Figures S1 and S2, and are further discussed in the discussion.

div.head: Discussion
div.p: The main ndings of the present study were that, during the rst week following discharge from CR, outpatients were signi cantly more physically active than control participants in a typical week. Motivational factors (i.e., perceived capability and affective attitudes toward PA) were associated with PA, and males spent more time in SB than females. However, no emotional-health related factors were signi cantly associated with PA and SB. This nding of higher PA levels in CR patients compared with healthy controls suggests that the rehabilitation program is effective in promoting PA levels at least in the short term-although this difference must be interpreted with caution because the groups differ on many demographic and motivational variables. However, we were unable to identify the key components of the intervention responsible for this effect.
During the rst week following discharge from CR, 88.2% of outpatients achieved the recommended 150 min of MVPA per week. These results are consistent with Bierbauer et al.

[8] ndings, which demonstrate that about 70% of patients succeeded in meeting PA recommendations in the rst three weeks following a CR program. Additionally, our ndings indicate that outpatients engaged in 18 min more of MVPA per day than control participants (p = .038). Although Barker et al.[38] have shown that individuals with cardiovascular disease remain less active than community-dwelling individuals without chronic disease, Steca et al. [39] demonstrated that the proportion of coronary patients who achieved the recommended PA level increased from 35.6% prior to the CR program to 60% six months after discharge. Thus, during the rst week of a CR program, patients tend to be more active than control participants as they are encouraged to improve their PA levels and reduce their SB during the CR program [3]. Finally, our estimation of outpatients meeting the PA guidelines after discharge from CR exceeded the literature (88.2%). This gap may also be due to a selection bias, as only 25% of the 68 included outpatients wore an accelerometer for one week at the end of the 6-week rehabilitation period.

At the beginning of the CR, outpatients had signi cantly lower perceived capabilities and affective attitudes toward PA and signi cantly higher levels of depressive symptoms, fatigue, and pain, compared to control participants. These ndings are consistent with current literature that highlights the high prevalence of pain, discomfort, and depression among cardiac patients [7,40]. Although we found signi cant differences in some deliberative motivational factors, such as perceived capability and affective attitudes, between outpatients and control participants, we did not nd any differences in the levels of automatic approach-avoidance tendencies toward PA and SB between the two groups. These results are di cult to compare to the existing literature, as to the best of our knowledge, no study has directly investigated and compared such automatic motivational factors between patients and control participants. Yet, it has been suggested that such automatic factors could be negatively biased in patients because of fear, pain, and discomfort felt during exercise [21,41,42]. For instance, the fear of PA, which is particularly pronounced in cardiac patients [43], may produce automatic avoidance tendencies toward PA [44]. The inability to observe differences in our study can be explained by several factors. First, patients enrolled in the IMPACT trial (i.e., a 6-week study aiming to improve their PA behaviors [21]) may have been more inclined to engage in regular PA than patients who were not interested in the study. Speci cally, although outpatients and control participants had different perceived capabilities and affective attitudes, both groups scored highly (> 4 out of 5 and > 8 out of 10, respectively). Second, the features of the task used to capture that approach-avoidance tendencies reactions may also explain the current ndings. Participants were asked to react to the format of the picture (portrait vs. landscape) rather than its content (avatar in active vs. passive behavior). This task has been found to produce smaller effect sizes compared to tasks that require a reaction to the content of the picture [45]. Consequently, while previous studies demonstrated that healthy participants exhibited a positive approach bias toward PA stimuli and a negative approach bias toward SB stimuli [46-50], our current results, as well as a recent fMRI study relying on the same task [51], failed to reproduce such observation in healthy participants.

No signi cant association was found between emotional health-related factors and device-measured MVPA during the rst week after discharge from CR, or during a typical week for control participants. These ndings differ from previous literature, indicating that patients experiencing pain, anxiety, depression, and fatigue were less physically active [7,[23][24][25]. For instance, Dagner et al. [7] found that patients with low anxiety and depression had higher odds of engaging in PA for more than 30 minutes per week following discharge from CR (OR = 0.6). Conversely, patients with high pain had a lower likelihood of engaging in PA (OR = 2.00). Additionally, Andersson et al. [24] found that individuals with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with high fatigue had lower odds of engaging in PA (OR = 2.33).

Our sensitivity analyses revealed that the current study had approximately 43% power to detect an odds ratio (OR) of 0.6, 65% power to detect an OR of 2.0 and 78% to detect an OR of 2.33 (Supplementary Material 9, Figure S2). Thus, this contrast could be explained in part by our low statistical power to detect the true effect.

In contrast to emotional health-related factors, several deliberative motivational factors were associated with MVPA. Speci cally, higher perceived capabilities, as well as stronger instrumental and affective attitudes toward PA, increased the odds of meeting the recommended levels of 150 min of MVPA per week. These results are consistent with Bermudez et al.'s study [2], indicating that patients exhibiting more positive affective attitudes toward PA were inclined to engage in higher PA levels after CR discharge. We found no evidence of a predictive effect of automatic approach-avoidance tendencies toward PA and SB on device-measured MVPA and sedentary behaviors in both cardiac patients and healthy control participants. These ndings contrast with previous work suggesting that automatic processes, including approach-avoidance tendencies, are instrumental to the regulation of PA behaviors [14][15][16]. For example, studies examining automatic processes have shown that PA cues attract attention [52][53][54], elicit positive affective responses, [20,55] and prompt approach tendencies [46, 50, 56], particularly in highly active individuals. These results suggest that automatic responses to PA cues that are not positive enough may partially explain the lack of engagement in PA. This lack of association in the present study can again be attributed to the task's characteristics, the relatively small sample size (N = 59) and the lack of statistical power. Therefore, before drawing de nite conclusion about the absence of association between approach-avoidance tendencies and PA and SB behaviors, additional wellpowered studies using different reaction-time tasks are needed.

Regarding device-based measured SB, male participants spent signi cantly more time in SB than female participants. Additionally, we observed a signi cant negative association between pain intensity and SB, indicating that higher pain intensity was linked to lower levels of SB. However, this association lost its signi cance after adjusting the model for participant type and sex (p = .139). This nding contrasts with O'Leary et al.'s study [57], which found a positive correlation between pain intensity and SB in rheumatoid arthritis patients (r = 0.31

). Similar to the present study, this association lost its signi cance when other factors, such as age and gender, were included in multivariate models. Overall, these results suggest that the in uence of PA-related motivational factors and emotional health-related factors is limited in explaining SB levels. However, it is important to note that most of the factors measured in this study related to PA and not to SB (e.g., perceived capabilities toward PA). Although the other studies have also used PA-based motivational measures to predict SB [58, 59], this feature may explain the lack of signi cant association. Future studies should investigate a wider range of factors that directly target SB, in order to better understand the in uence of motivational and emotional health-related factors on SB [58]. Finally, no signi cant interactions were observed between the motivational and emotional healthrelated predictors with levels of PA or SB and participant type (i.e., outpatient vs. control). Although this nding should be interpreted with caution given the rather small sample size of patients (n = 17), it could suggest that the motivational mechanisms underlying the regulation of PA behaviors may be identical between CR patients and community-dwelling individuals.

div.head: Constraints on Generality and Strengths
div.p: This study has several limitations that limit the generalizability of the ndings. First, it used a small sample size to measure PA and SB. The sample consisted of 17 CR patients and 42 community-dwelling participants, who had signi cantly different baseline characteristics. A larger sample of patients would provide more accurate estimations of PA and SB in this speci c population. Second, all patients involved in this study were enrolled in programs that took place at the Geneva University Hospitals, limiting the generalizability of the results to patients in other CR settings. Third, as it is common in longitudinal studies, we cannot dismiss the possibility of selective attrition bias. This means that patients who are more motivated to make lifestyle changes may be more likely to continue participating in this study compared to those who are less motivated. This bias may, for instance, account for the relatively high proportion of CR patients who were able to achieve the weekly recommended level of 150 min of MVPA. Consequently, future studies capable of retaining a larger proportion of patients may generate ndings that are more representative of the general population. Fourth, while we used device-based measures of SB with the Actigraph GT3X, int is worth noting that the activPal™ device has been identi ed as the most reliable device for measuring SB levels [60,61]. Fifth, despite observing signi cant associations between motivational factors, particularly affective attitudes, and PA behaviors, a large amount of variance remains to be explained. Therefore, the absence of predictive validity of the other motivational and emotional health-related factors needs to be interpreted with caution, as underpowered analyses may distort the size of the estimated effects [62,63].

Nonetheless, the study has several strengths that offset these limitations. First, the study incorporated a sample of CR patients along with a group of community-dwelling participants. This characteristic allowed for the observation of PA and SB in various contexts, including leisure time after discharge from CR and the daily lives of individuals without speci c medical care. Second, this study focused not only on PA but also on SB. While it is believed that both PA and SB have distinct impacts on the potential health bene ts of rehabilitation [11][12][13], few studies have explored these behaviors simultaneously. Third, this study utilized device-based measures for PA and SB, which render more reliable estimates than selfreported questionnaires [64][65][66]. Fourth, this study investigated the potential motivational factors that regulate PA and SB at both the deliberative (i.e., intention, perceived capabilities, and attitudes) and automatic (i.e., approach-avoidance tendencies) levels. Such research has been scarce in the existing literature and may offer a more comprehensive perspective on the determinants of these behaviors.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: The present study found that patients who had completed the outpatients CR program demonstrated higher levels of PA in their daily lives during the week following their discharge, compared to communitydwelling individuals. Additionally, perceived capabilities and instrumental and affective attitudes were signi cantly and positively associated with MVPA across all participants. These ndings support the implication of motivational factors in PA behaviors among both patients and community-dwelling individuals. Future interventions should be encouraged to target these factors to promote PA levels following CR programs. Although the nding suggests that the motivational mechanisms underlying the regulation of PA may be identical between patients and individuals without medical care, future studies with larger sample sizes are needed to provide more convincing evidence regarding this possibility. Finally, we encourage future studies investigating SB correlates among patients to include SB-speci c motivational factors (e.g., "During the next two weeks, I intend to spend no more than four hours in SB a day during my leisure-time.") and employ precise SB assessment tools such as activPal™. div.head: Acknowledgements
div.p: The authors are grateful to Arbnor Hasani, Auriane Emeline Micheli, Zoë Alicia Piazza of the University of Geneva and Anaïs Quossi of the University of Lyon for their implication on data collection. The authors are grateful to all study participants who volunteered, as well as the medical staff at Geneva University Hospitals for their assistance.
Funding L.F. is funded by the French Ministry of Higher Education, Research and Innovation. B.C. is supported by an Ambizione grant (PZ00P1_180040) from the Swiss National Science Foundation (SNSF).

div.head: Availability of Data and Materials
div.p: Deidenti ed data, data management, analysis codes and research materials have been made publicly available on Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.11072811).

div.head: Ethics Approval and Consent to Participate
div.p: The present study was in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki, and approved by the Ethics Committee of Geneva Canton, Switzerland (reference number: CCER2019-02257). Prior to participation in the study, all participants signed an informed consent form.

div.head: Consent for Publication
div.p: Consent for Publication declaration: not applicable.

div.head: Competing Interests
div.p: The authors have no con icts of interest relevant to this article to disclose.
